records.topic: What If You Jumped Into a Tunnel Through Earth?
records.hook: Fall through Earth, and you'd arrive in 38 minutes.
records.openingLine: Fall through Earth, and you'd arrive in 38 minutes.
records.secondBeat: Gravity pulls you down, then slows you back up.
records.scientificMechanism: inside a planet, gravity weakens toward the centre, so a falling object speeds up, then slows symmetrically on the way out
records.scenarioChange: a frictionless tunnel ran straight through Earth
records.expectedConsequence: a fall to the far side in under an hour; with air and friction you would oscillate and stop at the centre
records.coreQuestion: If you jumped into a tunnel through Earth, how long would the fall take, and where would you stop?
records.misconception: You wouldn't get stuck at the centre in a frictionless tunnel; you'd coast out the other side.
visualScenes: cutaway of Earth with a straight tunnel
speed curve peaking at the centre
uniform versus layered Earth density diagram
London to Paris shallow tunnel profile
editorialTitles: What If You Fell Through the Earth
Why a Fall Through Earth Takes 38 Minutes

facts.claim: By taking into account the realistic density distribution inside the Earth, the expected fall-through time is reduced from 42 to 38 minutes.
The straight line path between London and Paris would only require a maximum depth of 2.4 kilometres.
Such a tunnel would have an initial declination of 1.57 degrees.
The same idea was proposed, without calculation, by Lewis Carroll in 1893 in Sylvie and Bruno Concluded.

narration.text: Fall through Earth, and you'd arrive in 38 minutes.
Gravity pulls you down, then slows you back up.
For a uniform planet, the trip takes 42 minutes.
Earth's dense core speeds you up, cutting it to 38.
Even London to Paris would need only a 2.4-kilometre-deep tunnel.
Without air and friction, you'd pop out at the far side.
With them, you'd oscillate, then settle at the centre.
So gravity alone could run a train, if friction didn't exist.

records.topic: What If Ice Sank Instead of Floating?
records.hook: Ice floats because freezing water expands about 9%.
records.openingLine: Ice floats because freezing water expands about 9%.
records.secondBeat: Most substances shrink as they freeze. Water doesn't.
records.scientificMechanism: water expands as it freezes, so ice is less dense than liquid water and floats
records.scenarioChange: ice became denser than liquid water
records.expectedConsequence: lakes and seas would freeze from the bottom up, accumulating ice that summer could not reach
records.coreQuestion: If ice sank instead of floating, could lakes and oceans stay liquid?
records.misconception: Floating ice isn't normal behaviour; most solids are denser than their liquids.
visualScenes: density versus temperature curve peaking at 4 °C
lake freezing from the top down
lake freezing from the bottom up
fish under an insulating ice sheet
editorialTitles: What If Ice Sank
Why Floating Ice Keeps Lakes Alive

facts.claim: An unusual property of water is that its solid form is approximately 8.3% less dense than its liquid form; this is equivalent to a volumetric expansion of 9%.
The density of ice is 0.9167–0.9168 g/cm3 at 0 °C and standard atmospheric pressure, whereas water has a density of 0.9998–0.999863 g/cm3.
Liquid water is densest, essentially 1.00 g/cm3, at 4 °C.
When water freezes, it increases in volume (about 9% for fresh water).

narration.text: Ice floats because freezing water expands about 9%.
Most substances shrink as they freeze. Water doesn't.
Ice is about 8.3% less dense than liquid water.
Liquid water is densest at 4 °C.
If ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up.
Each winter's ice would pile up, shielded from summer sun.
Floating ice instead insulates the water beneath it.
So a strange quirk of water keeps lakes alive in winter.

records.topic: What If You Traveled Near the Speed of Light?
records.hook: Near light speed, your time almost stops.
records.openingLine: Near light speed, your time almost stops.
records.scientificMechanism: special relativity: moving clocks tick slower relative to a stationary observer, more so near light speed
records.scenarioChange: a traveller moved at a large fraction of light speed
records.expectedConsequence: the traveller ages far less than people at home; the effect is already measurable on the ISS
records.coreQuestion: If you traveled near the speed of light, how much slower would your time run?
records.misconception: Time dilation isn't science fiction; clocks on the ISS already measure it.
visualScenes: ISS orbiting with a clock readout
optical atomic clocks at two heights
editorialTitles: What Happens to Time Near Light Speed
Why Astronauts Come Home Slightly Younger

facts.claim: The faster the relative velocity, the greater the time dilation, with time slowing to a stop as one clock approaches the speed of light (299,792,458 m/s).
Time dilation of 0.5% may become important when an object approaches speeds on the order of 30,000 km/s (1/10 the speed of light).
After 6 months on the International Space Station, orbiting Earth at a speed of about 7,700 m/s, an astronaut will age about 5 milliseconds less than a person on Earth.
In 2010, gravitational time dilation was measured at the Earth's surface with a height difference of only 33 centimeters, using optical atomic clocks.

narration.text: Near light speed, your time almost stops.
Everyone else's keeps running normally.
Light moves at 299,792,458 metres per second.
At a tenth of that, time dilation reaches about 0.5%.
It's already real: 6 months on the ISS leaves astronauts 5 milliseconds younger.
Atomic clocks even detect gravity's version across 33 centimetres.
Near light speed, one year aboard could equal many years at home.
So speed doesn't just move you. It moves you through time.

records.topic: What If the 1859 Solar Superstorm Hit Today?
records.hook: Why a repeat of 1859 could cost $2.6 trillion.
records.openingLine: Why a repeat of 1859 could cost $2.6 trillion.
records.secondBeat: The 1859 Carrington storm set telegraph stations on fire.
records.scientificMechanism: a coronal mass ejection drives a geomagnetic storm that induces currents in long conductors on the ground
records.scenarioChange: a Carrington-class geomagnetic storm hit modern Earth
records.expectedConsequence: induced currents in power grids and damage to satellites, with economic costs in the hundreds of billions or more
records.coreQuestion: If the biggest solar storm on record hit today, what would fail first?
records.misconception: Solar storms don't harm people on the ground directly; the risk is to grids and satellites.
visualScenes: coronal mass ejection leaving the Sun
power grid transformers under induced current
editorialTitles: What If the Carrington Event Hit Today
Why a Solar Storm Would Hit Power Grids First

facts.claim: The Carrington Event was the most intense geomagnetic storm in recorded history, peaking on 1–2 September 1859 during solar cycle 10.
It created strong auroral displays that were reported globally and caused sparking and even fires in telegraph stations.
Telegraph systems all over Europe and North America failed, in some cases giving their operators electric shocks.
On 23 July 2012, a Carrington-class solar superstorm was observed, but its trajectory narrowly missed Earth by a margin of roughly nine days.
In June 2013, researchers at Lloyd's of London and AER estimated the cost of a similar event in the present to the US alone at US$600 billion to $2.6 trillion.

narration.text: Why a repeat of 1859 could cost $2.6 trillion.
The 1859 Carrington storm set telegraph stations on fire.
Telegraph systems across Europe and North America failed.
Some operators even got electric shocks.
In 2012, a similar storm missed Earth by about 9 days.
A 2013 estimate put a repeat's U.S. cost at $600 billion to $2.6 trillion.
Today, long power lines and satellites would take the hit.
So the same storm would cost far more now than then.

records.topic: What If Asteroid Apophis Hit Earth?
records.hook: Apophis once had a 2.7% chance of hitting Earth.
records.openingLine: Apophis once had a 2.7% chance of hitting Earth.
records.secondBeat: Better tracking ruled out an impact in 2029.
records.scientificMechanism: repeated tracking shrinks an asteroid's orbital uncertainty until an impact can be confirmed or ruled out
records.scenarioChange: Apophis were on a collision course
records.expectedConsequence: a regional disaster rather than a global one; instead, its 2029 flyby becomes a planetary-defence test
records.coreQuestion: If Apophis hit Earth, how bad would it be, and why are we sure it won't in 2029?
records.misconception: Apophis won't hit Earth in 2029; it will pass closer than geostationary satellites.
visualScenes: 2029 flyby path inside the satellite ring
editorialTitles: What If Apophis Hit Earth
Why Apophis Will Miss Us in 2029

facts.claim: 99942 Apophis is a near-Earth asteroid and a potentially hazardous object, 450 metres (1,480 ft) by 170 metres (560 ft) in size.
During a brief period of concern in December 2004, initial observations indicated a probability of 2.7% that the asteroid would hit Earth on Friday, April 13, 2029.
It will pass Earth in 2029 at a distance of about 31,600 km (19,600 mi) above the surface.
By 2021, the uncertainty in the 2029 approach distance had been reduced from hundreds of kilometres to just a couple of kilometres.
Geostationary orbit lies 35,786 km (22,236 mi) above the Earth's equator.

narration.text: Apophis once had a 2.7% chance of hitting Earth.
Better tracking ruled out an impact in 2029.
The asteroid is about 450 metres long.
In 2029, it passes just 31,600 kilometres above the surface.
That's inside the 35,786-kilometre ring of geostationary satellites.
Its path is now known to within a couple of kilometres.
A hit would devastate a region, not end civilisation.
So Apophis turned from a threat into a planetary-defence rehearsal.

records.topic: What If Olympus Mons Stood on Earth?
records.hook: Why Earth couldn't hold a volcano 2.5 times Everest.
records.openingLine: Why Earth couldn't hold a volcano 2.5 times Everest.
records.secondBeat: Mars's Olympus Mons stands about 21 kilometres high.
records.scientificMechanism: a volcano's maximum height depends on surface gravity and on whether the crust stays over the same hotspot
records.scenarioChange: Mars's Olympus Mons were placed on Earth
records.expectedConsequence: Earth's stronger gravity and moving plates could not support or build a volcano that large
records.coreQuestion: If Olympus Mons stood on Earth, could our planet even hold it up?
records.misconception: Olympus Mons isn't a steep peak; its flanks average only a 5% slope.
visualScenes: Olympus Mons beside Everest to scale
editorialTitles: What If Olympus Mons Were on Earth
Why Mars Has the Solar System's Giant Volcano

facts.claim: As measured by the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter, it is 21.287 kilometres (69,840 ft) high, about 2.5 times the elevation of Mount Everest above sea level.
The edifice is about 600 km (370 mi) wide.
Olympus Mons covers an area of about 300,000 km2, which is approximately the size of Italy or the Philippines, and it is supported by a 70 km thick lithosphere.
The average slope on the volcano's flanks is only 5%.

narration.text: Why Earth couldn't hold a volcano 2.5 times Everest.
Mars's Olympus Mons stands about 21 kilometres high.
It's about 600 kilometres wide, the size of Italy in area.
Its average slope is only 5%.
So standing on it, you'd barely notice you're on a mountain.
On Earth, crust this tall would sink and crumble under its weight.
Mars' weaker gravity and still crust let it grow.
So the Solar System's giant volcano needed a smaller planet.

records.topic: What If the Sun Ran Out of Hydrogen?
records.hook: The Sun has 5 billion years of core hydrogen.
records.openingLine: The Sun has 5 billion years of core hydrogen.
records.secondBeat: Then fusion there stops, and the core contracts.
records.scientificMechanism: when core hydrogen fusion stops, the core contracts and heats while the outer layers expand into a red giant
records.scenarioChange: the Sun's core exhausted its hydrogen
records.expectedConsequence: the Sun becomes a red giant; long before, its slow brightening makes Earth uninhabitable
records.coreQuestion: If the Sun ran out of hydrogen, what would happen to Earth, and when?
records.misconception: The Sun won't explode as a supernova; it isn't massive enough.
visualScenes: red giant swelling past inner orbits
editorialTitles: What Happens When the Sun Runs Out of Fuel
Why We Live in the Sun's Calm Middle Age

facts.claim: The Sun's mass is around 330,000 times that of Earth, making up about 99.86% of the total mass of the Solar System.
The Sun formed approximately 4.6 billion years ago from the gravitational collapse of matter within a region of a large molecular cloud.
The Sun will spend a total of approximately 10 to 11 billion years as a main-sequence star before the red giant phase of the Sun.
When it runs out of hydrogen in the core in approximately 5 billion years, core hydrogen fusion will stop, and there will be nothing to prevent the core from contracting.

narration.text: The Sun has 5 billion years of core hydrogen.
Then fusion there stops, and the core contracts.
It holds 99.86% of the Solar System's mass.
It's about 4.6 billion years old, roughly halfway through.
Next comes the red giant phase.
The Sun will swell, and the inner planets will face its heat.
Earth's oceans will be long gone before then.
So we're living in the Sun's calm middle age.

records.topic: What If You Stood at the Bottom of the Mariana Trench?
records.hook: Why only a few have reached 10,920 metres down.
records.openingLine: Why only a few have reached 10,920 metres down.
records.secondBeat: The Challenger Deep is the ocean's deepest point.
records.scientificMechanism: water pressure rises by roughly one atmosphere every ten metres of depth
records.scenarioChange: a person reached the Challenger Deep without a pressure hull
records.expectedConsequence: air-filled spaces in the body would collapse instantly; only thick-walled vehicles survive there
records.coreQuestion: If you stood at the bottom of the Mariana Trench, what would the pressure do to you?
records.misconception: The deepest ocean isn't lifeless; simple organisms thrive in its sediment.
visualScenes: depth profile to the Challenger Deep
Everest upside down in the trench
editorialTitles: What If You Went to the Bottom of the Ocean
Why the Mariana Trench Crushes Us but Not Life

facts.claim: Both the western and eastern basins have recorded depths (by sonar bathymetry) in excess of 10,920 metres (35,827 ft).
The first descent by any vehicle was conducted by the United States Navy using the bathyscaphe Trieste in January 1960.
The steel walls were 12.7 cm (5.0 in) thick and designed to withstand pressure of up to 1250 kilograms per square centimetre (17800 psi; 1210 atm; 123 MPa).
An analysis of the sediment samples collected by Kaiko found large numbers of simple organisms at 10,900 m (35,800 ft).
Cameron decided to start the ascent to the surface after only 2 hours and 34 minutes.

narration.text: Why only a few have reached 10,920 metres down.
The Challenger Deep is the ocean's deepest point.
Trieste first reached the bottom in January 1960.
Its steel hull was 12.7 centimetres thick.
It was built to withstand 1,210 atmospheres of pressure.
Unprotected, that pressure would crush every air space in your body.
Yet simple organisms thrive in the sediment at 10,900 metres.
So the deepest place on Earth is hostile to us, not to life.

records.topic: What If You Lived in Space for a Year?
records.hook: In space, your bones lose about 1.5% a month.
records.openingLine: In space, your bones lose about 1.5% a month.
records.secondBeat: Muscles can shrink even faster without gravity.
records.scientificMechanism: without gravity loading, the body stops maintaining bone and muscle it no longer needs
records.scenarioChange: a person lived in orbit for a year
records.expectedConsequence: steady bone loss, rapid muscle loss, circulation and vision changes, and added radiation risk
records.coreQuestion: If you lived in space for a year, what would weightlessness take from your body?
records.misconception: Weightlessness isn't restful for the body; bone and muscle start wasting within days.
visualScenes: blood flow in the neck veins
editorialTitles: What a Year in Space Does to Your Body
Why Mars Crews Must Fight Weightlessness

facts.claim: This results in a loss of bone tissue approximately 1.5% per month especially from the lower vertebrae, hip, and femur.
facts.source: Wikipedia — Effect of spaceflight on the human body

facts.claim: Some muscles atrophy rapidly, and without regular exercise astronauts can lose up to 20% of their muscle mass in just 5 to 11 days.
facts.source: Wikipedia — Effect of spaceflight on the human body

facts.claim: In November 2019, researchers reported that astronauts experienced serious blood flow and clot problems while on board the ISS, based on a six-month study of 11 healthy astronauts.
facts.source: Wikipedia — Effect of spaceflight on the human body

facts.claim: A 2024 assessment noted that well-known problems include bone loss, heightened cancer risk, vision impairment, weakened immune systems, and mental health issues.
facts.source: Wikipedia — Effect of spaceflight on the human body

narration.text: In space, your bones lose about 1.5% a month.
Muscles can shrink even faster without gravity.
Without exercise, astronauts can lose up to 20% of muscle in 5 to 11 days.
Hips, spine and thighs lose bone the fastest.
A 2019 study found blood-flow and clot problems on the ISS.
Vision problems and cancer risk add to the list.
So a year in orbit trains the body to forget gravity.
That's the real obstacle for any trip to Mars.

records.topic: What If a Mountain Fell Into a Bay?
records.hook: Why water once climbed 524 metres up a mountain.
records.openingLine: Why water once climbed 524 metres up a mountain.
records.secondBeat: 30 million cubic metres of rock caused it.
records.scientificMechanism: a large rockslide into a confined bay displaces water violently, driving extreme run-up on the opposite shore
records.scenarioChange: a massive rockslide plunged into a narrow bay
records.expectedConsequence: a local megatsunami strips slopes hundreds of metres up, far beyond any earthquake-driven wave
records.coreQuestion: If a mountain fell into a bay, how high could the water climb?
records.misconception: The tallest waves on record weren't caused by earthquakes directly but by landslides.
visualScenes: run-up line on the far slope
earthquake fault trace along the bay
editorialTitles: The Wave That Climbed 524 Metres
Why Landslides Make the Tallest Waves

facts.claim: The 1958 Lituya Bay earthquake occurred on July 9, 1958, with a moment magnitude of 7.8 to 8.3.
facts.source: Wikipedia — 1958 Lituya Bay earthquake and megatsunami

facts.claim: Over 30 million cubic meters of rock fell from a height of several hundred meters into the bay, creating a megatsunami.
facts.source: Wikipedia — 1958 Lituya Bay earthquake and megatsunami

facts.claim: The wave caused damage to the vegetation up the headlands around the area where the rockfall occurred, up to a height of 524 meters.
facts.source: Wikipedia — 1958 Lituya Bay earthquake and megatsunami

facts.claim: Lituya Bay is a T-shaped bay with a width of 2 miles (3 km) and a length of 7 miles (11 km).
facts.source: Wikipedia — 1958 Lituya Bay earthquake and megatsunami

facts.claim: A 1:675 recreation of the tsunami found the wave crest was 150 m (490 ft) tall.
facts.source: Wikipedia — 1958 Lituya Bay earthquake and megatsunami

narration.text: Why water once climbed 524 metres up a mountain.
30 million cubic metres of rock caused it.
An earthquake of magnitude 7.8 to 8.3 shook it loose.
Lituya Bay is only 3 kilometres wide.
The water surged up the far slope, stripping soil and trees.
Models put the wave crest itself at about 150 metres.
A narrow bay concentrates a landslide's push into one giant surge.
So the tallest waves come from falling mountains, not earthquakes alone.

records.topic: What If Another Tambora Erupted Today?
records.hook: Under 1 °C of cooling cancelled a whole summer.
records.openingLine: Under 1 °C of cooling cancelled a whole summer.
records.secondBeat: Tambora erupted in 1815. Summer 1816 barely came.
records.scientificMechanism: a large eruption injects sulfur into the stratosphere, forming aerosols that reflect sunlight and cool the globe
records.expectedConsequence: a cool year of failed harvests, transmitted worldwide through food trade and prices
records.coreQuestion: If another Tambora erupted today, could a single volcano still cancel summer?
records.misconception: It didn't take a huge global cooling to cause famine; less than 1 °C was enough.
visualScenes: shipping routes spreading a food shortage
editorialTitles: The Volcano That Cancelled Summer
What If Tambora Erupted Today

facts.claim: The year 1816 is known as the Year Without a Summer because of severe climate abnormalities that caused average global temperatures to decrease by 0.4–0.7 °C (0.7–1 °F).
The main cause of the Year Without a Summer is generally held to be a volcanic winter created by the April 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora on Sumbawa.
Between 1816 and 1819, major typhus epidemics occurred in parts of Europe, including Ireland, Italy, Switzerland, and Scotland, precipitated by the famine.
The ice dam collapsed catastrophically in June 1818, killing forty people in the resulting flood.

narration.text: Under 1 °C of cooling cancelled a whole summer.
Tambora erupted in 1815. Summer 1816 barely came.
Global temperatures dropped by 0.4 to 0.7 °C.
That small shift was enough to ruin harvests.
Famine helped trigger typhus epidemics across Europe until 1819.
Today, a similar eruption would hit global grain markets at once.
Food trade would spread the shortage, and the price shock, worldwide.
So a single volcano could still test the world's food supply.

records.topic: What If the Mediterranean Sea Dried Up?
records.hook: Why the Mediterranean once lost 3,300 km³ a year.
records.openingLine: Why the Mediterranean once lost 3,300 km³ a year.
records.secondBeat: It left a basin up to 5 kilometres deep.
records.scientificMechanism: a nearly enclosed sea in a dry climate loses more water to evaporation than rivers and rain supply
records.scenarioChange: the Mediterranean was cut off from the Atlantic
records.expectedConsequence: the sea evaporates into a deep salt basin until Gibraltar reopens and refills it
records.coreQuestion: If the Mediterranean dried up, how fast would it go, and what would bring it back?
records.misconception: The Mediterranean drying out isn't hypothetical; it happened, possibly several times.
visualScenes: Mediterranean basin drained to salt flats
thick salt layers in a core
depth map 5 km below sea level
editorialTitles: When the Mediterranean Dried Up
Why One Strait Decides Whether a Sea Exists

facts.claim: This massive desiccation left a deep dry basin, reaching 3 to 5 km (1.9 to 3.1 mi) deep below normal sea level, with a few hypersaline pockets.
When that was shut off sometime between 6.5 to 6 MYBP, net evaporative loss set in at the rate of around 3,300 cubic kilometres yearly.
The Messinian salinity crisis ended with the Strait of Gibraltar finally reopening 5.33 Ma, when the Atlantic rapidly filled up the Mediterranean basin in what is known as the Zanclean flood.
The Sorbas Basin was filled with evaporites at 5.5 million years ago (Ma), compared to the main basin at 5.96 Ma.
Research has suggested that the desiccation-flooding cycle may have repeated several times during the last 630,000 years of the Miocene epoch.

narration.text: Why the Mediterranean once lost 3,300 km³ a year.
It left a basin up to 5 kilometres deep.
Cut off from the Atlantic, evaporation outpaced every river.
Salt piled up in thick layers across the seabed.
The drying and flooding may have repeated several times.
It ended 5.33 million years ago, when Gibraltar reopened.
The Atlantic poured back in, in the Zanclean flood.
So one narrow strait decides whether a sea exists.

records.hook: Why Krakatoa was heard 4,800 kilometres away.
records.openingLine: Why Krakatoa was heard 4,800 kilometres away.
records.secondBeat: That's Indonesia to an island near Mauritius.
records.scientificMechanism: an explosive eruption and caldera collapse send pressure waves around the globe and tsunamis across nearby coasts
records.expectedConsequence: tsunamis along the Sunda Strait coasts and regional air travel halted by ash
records.coreQuestion: If Krakatoa erupted today, what would do the most damage: the blast, the ash or the waves?
records.misconception: Most of Krakatoa's deaths came from tsunamis, not the explosion itself.
visualScenes: sound reach circles to Perth and Rodrigues
editorialTitles: What If Krakatoa Erupted Today
Why Krakatoa's Waves Were Deadlier Than Its Bang

facts.claim: The explosion was heard 3,110 kilometres (1,930 mi) away in Perth, Western Australia, and Rodrigues near Mauritius, 4,800 kilometres (3,000 mi) away.
At least 36,417 deaths are attributed to the eruption and the tsunamis it created.
By 2:00 p.m., a black ash cloud could be seen 27 km (89,000 ft) high.
Explosions could be heard in Batavia (Jakarta) 160 km (100 mi) away, rattling windows and doors.

narration.text: Why Krakatoa was heard 4,800 kilometres away.
That's Indonesia to an island near Mauritius.
In Perth, 3,110 kilometres away, people heard it too.
Its ash cloud climbed 27 kilometres high.
At least 36,417 deaths are linked to the eruption and tsunamis.
Today, coasts around the Sunda Strait would face the waves first.
Ash high in the sky would ground flights across the region.
So Krakatoa's real danger was its waves, not its bang.

records.topic: What If Fusion Power Actually Worked?
records.hook: Why fusion's 54% surplus isn't electricity yet.
records.openingLine: Why fusion's 54% surplus isn't electricity yet.
records.secondBeat: At NIF, a 2.05 MJ laser shot yielded 3.15 MJ.
records.scientificMechanism: inertial confinement fusion: lasers compress a fuel capsule until hydrogen isotopes fuse and release energy
records.expectedConsequence: scientific breakeven is proven; engineering gain, repetition rate and cost remain the barriers
records.coreQuestion: If fusion power actually worked, what's still standing between a lab shot and your electricity?
records.misconception: Fusion breakeven at NIF counted laser energy on target, not the power the facility drew from the grid.
visualScenes: 192 laser beams converging on a capsule
energy in versus out bar chart
editorialTitles: What It Will Take for Fusion Power to Work
Why Fusion Breakeven Isn't Electricity Yet

facts.claim: The design uses 192 beamlines in a parallel system of flashlamp-pumped, neodymium-doped phosphate glass lasers.
The feat required a 2.05 MJ laser (up from 1.9 MJ in 2021), yielding 3.15 MJ, a 54% surplus.
On December 5, 2022, NIF reached scientific breakeven for the first time, producing 154% of the energy of the laser.
Subsequent shots have seen continued increases in yield; a February 2024 shot exceeded 5 MJ.

narration.text: Why fusion's 54% surplus isn't electricity yet.
At NIF, a 2.05 MJ laser shot yielded 3.15 MJ.
It was the first scientific breakeven, using 192 laser beams.
A 2024 shot pushed yield past 5 megajoules.
But the lasers drew far more power from the grid than that.
A power plant would need far higher gain, many times a second.
Scientific breakeven is proof of physics, not yet of electricity.
So fusion works. Making it pay is the next problem.

records.topic: What If We Dimmed the Sun to Cool Earth?
records.hook: One volcano cooled Earth by 0.5 °C for years.
records.openingLine: One volcano cooled Earth by 0.5 °C for years.
records.secondBeat: Some scientists propose copying it on purpose.
records.scientificMechanism: sulfate aerosols in the stratosphere reflect part of incoming sunlight, cooling the surface
records.scenarioChange: humans injected aerosols into the stratosphere on purpose
records.expectedConsequence: cheap, fast cooling that leaves carbon dioxide untouched and must be maintained indefinitely
records.coreQuestion: If we dimmed the Sun to cool Earth, what would we gain, and what could go wrong?
records.misconception: Dimming sunlight wouldn't remove any carbon dioxide; stopping it would release the masked warming.
editorialTitles: What If We Dimmed the Sun
Why Geoengineering Treats the Fever, Not the Cause

facts.claim: For example, the eruption of Mount Pinatubo in 1991 caused global temperatures to drop by about 0.5 degrees Celsius for up to three years.
The annual cost of delivering a sufficient amount of sulfur to counteract expected greenhouse warming is estimated at $5–10 billion US dollars.
In comparison, the annual cost estimates for climate damage or emission mitigation range from US$200 billion to 2 trillion.
From 1850 to 2014, they reduced global average surface temperature by about 0.66 °C.

narration.text: One volcano cooled Earth by 0.5 °C for years.
Some scientists propose copying it on purpose.
Its sulfur haze reflected sunlight back to space.
Estimates put a yearly program at $5 to 10 billion.
Climate damage costs are estimated at $200 billion to $2 trillion a year.
But stopping suddenly would unleash the hidden warming fast.
And it wouldn't remove any carbon dioxide at all.
So dimming the sun treats the fever, not the infection.

records.topic: What If a Magnetar Came Close to Earth?
records.hook: Why one star's magnetism outweighs lead 10,000 times.
records.openingLine: Why one star's magnetism outweighs lead 10,000 times.
records.secondBeat: Its field packs more mass-energy than solid metal.
records.scientificMechanism: a magnetar's field is so intense that it deforms atoms and stores more energy per volume than matter's mass density
records.scenarioChange: a magnetar passed near the Solar System
records.expectedConsequence: at close range its field would distort atoms themselves; even from afar its flares reach Earth
records.coreQuestion: If a magnetar came close to Earth, what would its magnetic field do to ordinary matter?
records.misconception: A magnetar's danger isn't just attraction of metal; its field distorts atoms themselves.
editorialTitles: What If a Magnetar Came Close
Why a Magnetar Could Stretch Atoms

facts.claim: Earth has a geomagnetic field of 30–60 microteslas, and a neodymium-based, rare-earth magnet has a field of about 1.25 tesla.
A magnetar's field has an energy density with an E/c2 mass density more than 10,000 times that of lead.
Magnetars are formed by the collapse of a star with a mass 10–25 times that of the Sun.
Starquakes on the surface of the magnetar often lead to extremely powerful gamma-ray flare emissions which have been recorded on Earth in 1979, 1998, and 2004.

narration.text: Why one star's magnetism outweighs lead 10,000 times.
Its field packs more mass-energy than solid metal.
Earth's field is just 30 to 60 microteslas.
A strong neodymium magnet reaches about 1.25 tesla.
Near a magnetar, atoms themselves stretch into thin rods.
Starquakes there have sent gamma-ray flares all the way to Earth.
Up close, chemistry itself would stop working.
So the strongest magnets in the universe are also the deadliest.

records.topic: What If All the Bees Disappeared?

facts.claim: An estimated 87.5% of the world's flowering plant species are animal-pollinated, and 60% of crop plant species use animal pollinators.
According to the USDA 80% of insect crop pollination in the US is due to honey bees.
The expected direct reduction in total agricultural production in the US in the absence of animal pollination is expected to be 3 to 8%.
A 2000 study about the economic effects of the honey bee on US food crops calculated that it helped to produce US$14.6 billion in monetary value.

narration.text: 87.5% of flowering plants rely on animal pollinators.
Bees are the best known, but not the only ones.
About 60% of crop species use animal pollinators too.
In the US, honey bees do 80% of insect crop pollination.
Yet losing all animal pollinators would cut US farm output only 3 to 8%.
Staples like wheat and rice are pollinated by wind.
The real losses would be fruits, nuts and vegetables.
So without bees we'd still eat, just with far less variety.
